sentences.text:
This petition has been preferred by the applicant/State against the judgment dated 22.12.2014 passed by Additional Sessions Judge, Nagod, District-Satna (MP) in Sessions Trial No.349/2013,
whereby learned trial Court has acquitted the accused (respondent herein) of the charges under Sections 376, 450 of Indian Penal Code.
Assailing the aforesaid judgment, this petition under Section 378(III) of CrPC for grant of leave to appeal has been filed.
2. It is contended by learned counsel appearing for State that impugned judgment of acquittal passed by learned Trial Court is incorrect, improper, and bad in law.
The procedure adopted by learned NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:9368 2 MCRC-38-2016 Trial Court is contrary to the evidence and material available on record and is perverse.
It is also contended that learned Trial Court has failed to properly appreciate the evidence on record and has erroneously acquitted the respondent.
The prosecution has proved the commission of the offence beyond reasonable doubt, and the testimony of prosecution witnesses fully supports and corroborates the case of prosecution.
Consequently, impugned judgment is liable to be set aside, and the accused (respondent herein) deserves to be convicted in accordance with law.

3. Heard learned counsel for the State and perused the material available on record.

sentences.text: This petition has been filed with a delay of 264 days.
No plausible or satisfactory explanation has been offered, nor has any document been produced, to show sufficient cause for not filing the petition within the prescribed period.
The applicant's approach in seeking condonation of delay is casual and lacks bona fides.
In the absence of any just and reasonable explanation for such an inordinate delay, no case for condoning the delay in filing present petition is made out.

Accordingly,
I.A. No.21/2016 filed under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is dismissed.
5. Even otherwise, and without entering into the merits in detail, a perusal of the record does not disclose any infirmity warranting interference.

Upon a careful examination of the statement of the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:9368 3 MCRC-38-2016 prosecutrix, it is evident that she alleged that the accused had sexual intercourse with her on the alleged date of the incident.
However, in paragraph 8 of her cross-examination, she admitted that she did not raise any alarm at the relevant time.
She further did not allege before the Magistrate under Section 164 CrPC that the accused had gagged her during the alleged act.
This constitutes a material omission in her police statement (Exhibit-D/1).
The prosecutrix also admitted that she did not immediately disclose the incident to her parents and the disclosure was made at a belated stage, only after she was carrying a fetus of 7-8 months.
Such conduct is admissible under Section 8 of the Indian Evidence Act and is relevant in assessing the probability of consent.
6. Further, Vimla Chaudhary (P.W.-2) stated that upon enquiring about the pregnancy, the prosecutrix informed her that the accused was responsible.

In paragraph 7 of her cross-examination,
the said witness clarified that the prosecutrix did not disclose the incident on her own, but only after being questioned and that too after the pregnancy had become apparent.
No independent witness has corroborated the version of the prosecutrix.
The DNA report is also absent.
Furthermore, no documentary evidence has been produced to establish that the prosecutrix was a minor at the time of the alleged incident.
Thus, upon overall appreciation of the evidence on record, the statements clearly indicate that the prosecutrix was a consenting party.
The prosecution has failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:9368 4 MCRC-38-2016 7.
Perusal of the impugned order reflects that learned Trial Court has duly considered all the evidence adduced by the prosecution.

Learned Trial Court has rightly appreciated the evidence on record and has acquitted the accused on the ground that the evidence produced by the prosecution is mutually inconsistent and does not inspire confidence.
The Trial Court has meticulously examined the testimony of the witnesses, the surrounding circumstances, and the material on record, and no infirmity is discernible in the order of acquittal.
The evidence on record, as rightly noted by the learned Trial Court, has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt against the accused.
The prosecution has failed to establish the guilt of the accused through credible, consistent, and reliable evidence.
In view of the aforesaid, the acquittal recorded by the Trial Court cannot be said to be perverse, irregular, or contrary to law.
8. Consequently, present petition seeking grant of leave to appeal, being hopelessly time-barred and devoid of merit, stands dismissed.
